A specific texture associated with the event

I dwell on what other people have done to me
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

issues.item: Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Unfamiliar Places' is an avoidance/safety behaviour rather than a threat appraisal item. In this profile, the Threat node otherwise contains felt current danger and reliving; this item is misclassified and weakens within-node coherence.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Authority Figures' is not phrased as a strategy and appears to describe a trigger category. It is also weakly supported by the rest of the profile, since no memory, threat, or appraisal content specifically involves authorities or uniforms. This creates a cross-node mismatch and a node-level inconsistency within Maladaptive Strategies.

vignette:
Layla keeps the windows of her work van open, even in the winter, preferring the bite of the cold to the risk of silence. At fifty-five, she has worked as an HVAC technician for nearly two decades, a master of airflow and temperature, yet she cannot regulate the climate inside her own mind. The trouble, which began thirty years ago on a storm-tossed sea, has recently become unbearable. It was a memory she had tried to bury under the steady routine of a new life in a new country, but it refused to stay submerged. The crossing was a blur of terror and hope, a hundred souls crammed onto a fishing boat not meant for fifty. The memory returns to her not as a coherent story but as a series of punishing sensory fragments: the heaving grey water, the relentless uncertainty of each passing hour, and the rough, damp texture of the canvas tarp she and her younger brother huddled under.

A recent call to a house with a flooded basement brought it all back with the force of the original storm. The moment she saw the dark water pooling on the concrete floor, the past became the present (Triggers -> Memory). She was no longer in a suburban home but back on the boat, the overwhelming feeling of dread so powerful she had to brace herself against the doorframe. The memory itself is a source of profound shame; she remembers her own paralysis, the feeling of being small and helpless while others were brave. When these images surface, the event feels so extreme, so beyond the pale of normal life, that a part of her still finds it hard to believe it actually happened to her. This sense of unreality is immediately followed by a wave of raw fear, a certainty that disaster is imminent (Memory -> Threat). Her body reacts before her mind can catch up; she suddenly feels as if she is back on the unstable deck, scanning the churning waves for a threat she can neither name nor fight.

In the grip of this terror, her first and only impulse is to find a way out. The memory of being trapped, with nowhere to run, has forged in her an iron-clad set of rules for survival (Memory -> Maladaptive Strategies). Before entering any building-a client's home, a grocery store, even the local library-she must first locate all the exits. She finds herself constantly scanning her surroundings, her eyes sweeping over rooms not for HVAC units but for potential dangers. This constant vigilance, this relentless mapping of escape routes, has become a secondary, full-time job. Her focus on survival strategies keeps the original trauma perpetually in mind; planning her escape from a two-story colonial home invariably brings back the suffocating memory of having no escape at all from the open ocean (Maladaptive Strategies -> Memory).

These very strategies, meant to keep her safe, have become the architects of her prison. The constant scanning for danger ensures her world remains a threatening place, reinforcing the belief that she is never truly secure (Maladaptive Strategies -> Threat). An unusual quiet, like the moment the boat's engine sputtered and died, now feels like a prelude to catastrophe. This heightened sense of threat acts as its own trigger, a feedback loop where a moment of silence in her apartment can send her spiraling back into the memory of that terrifying stillness on the water before the screaming began (Threat -> Memory). Furthermore, her hypervigilance makes her exquisitely sensitive to the very things she dreads. By always checking her environment, she is far more likely to notice a puddle on the sidewalk or a coarse-textured blanket on a sofa, details that immediately reactivate the trauma (Maladaptive Strategies -> Triggers).

Over the years, the memories have made her world smaller, sensitizing her to more and more triggers (Memory -> Triggers). What began as a fear of the ocean has expanded to include basements, heavy rain, and even the texture of certain fabrics. At night, she finds herself dwelling on the men who took their money for the unsafe passage, a bitter rumination that stokes the fires of the past. Her boss has spoken to her twice about her pace, about the time she takes on-site before even beginning a job. Layla couldn't explain that she was not procrastinating, but securing the perimeter. She finally sought help after a new client, a young mother, found her meticulously checking the window latches in a nursery and asked, with gentle concern, if everything was alright. In that moment, Layla saw the chasm between her inner world of constant threat and the quiet reality of a suburban afternoon. She came to therapy not hoping for a life without memories, but for a life where a memory is just that, and where silence can simply be peace.
